book.title: Z80: The Amazing Processor of the 1970s
book.author: c64spark

sections.title: A World of Wire and Iron
sections.content:
Imagine an engineer in 1968. Not a purchasing manager, not an accountant — a design engineer sitting at a desk covered in component catalogs. His mission: to build the controller for a new factory machine. A system for automated counting and packaging, let's say.

Until yesterday, the previous version of this machine had been built with hundreds of TTL chips and thousands of hand-soldered wires. Today, the factory manager has issued a new order: the new machine must be twice as fast, have more memory, and print a daily report. Our engineer looks at the design he drew up last month, and he knows — he has to start over from scratch. The old board is useless now. Hardwired logic, like lines carved into stone, cannot be changed. He must design a new board, with a fresh arrangement of chips — and if a new requirement arises tomorrow, this board, too, will be thrown onto the scrap heap of history.

This was the true nightmare of the electronics industry in the 1960s: disposable logic. Every new product demanded new hardware. Every small change in function meant redesigning the printed circuit board, rewiring everything, and months of testing. The cost of designing custom hardware for every single application was a boulder chained to the ankle of innovation.

On a larger scale, the manufacturers of big computers were struggling with another version of the same disease. Every new model from DEC or IBM had its own unique internal architecture. But their main problem wasn't software incompatibility — that was the customer's headache, not the manufacturer's. The manufacturers' own problem was exactly the same as that of the factory controller engineer: designing new hardware for every generation, on a massive scale, at staggering cost. Locking the customer into a closed ecosystem was a side effect of this situation — not the root cause.

Inside Fairchild Semiconductor, a spark was forming. A young engineer named Ted Hoff, working on memory chip designs, had grown sick of this vicious cycle. In conversation with his colleague Stanley Mazor, he floated an idea that, at first glance, seemed almost naive: "Why scatter the logic of computation across dozens of chips? Why not gather all of it into a single chip? A central chip that could play the role of a brain for any device, simply by executing different instructions?"

Hoff's idea was to separate "operational logic" from "physical hardware." Instead of designing a dedicated electronic board with fixed wiring for every product, a standard chip could play any role by reading instructions stored in memory. Today, a packaging controller. Tomorrow, a calculator. The day after, a fire alarm system. The hardware stayed the same; it was the software that changed.

The idea went nowhere at Fairchild. But fate had other plans.

In 1969, a Japanese company named Busicom approached Intel — which had just broken away from Fairchild — with an order to design a set of twelve custom chips for an advanced desktop calculator. Ted Hoff, now at Intel, instead of following the original plan, made Busicom a revolutionary counterproposal: instead of twelve chips, let's design four. Let one of them be a central processing unit that handles all the calculations. By changing the program stored in memory, the same hardware could perform entirely different tasks.

Busicom's managers, after a brief hesitation, agreed. And so the work began.

Hoff and Mazor designed the logical architecture on paper. But turning this design into an actual chip on silicon was a task bordering on miracle. This is where two decisive figures entered the story: Federico Faggin, an Italian engineer who had just joined Intel and was a peerless master of physical chip design; and Masatoshi Shima, a Japanese engineer from Busicom who implemented the digital logic with obsessive precision. Faggin would later say: "Without Shima, the 4004 would never have been built." It was this four-man team — Hoff, Mazor, Shima, and Faggin — who brought the world's first commercial microprocessor into existence.

On November 15, 1971, Intel introduced the 4004: a 4-bit chip with 2,300 transistors. On the surface, it was just a faster brain for advanced calculators. But beneath the surface, it carried a revolutionary concept: universal programmable control. For the first time, "what a device does" had been separated from "how it is physically wired."

In the months that followed, creative engineers in corners of the world began discovering this concept. In major cities, traffic light controllers — once cabinets full of relays and wires — were now running on a single 4004 and a memory chip. Changing the traffic pattern no longer required dispatching an engineering team for rewiring; you simply swapped the memory chip for one with the new program. A quiet, invisible revolution was unfolding inside medical devices, industrial controllers, and security systems.

sections.title: A Bridge to the Personal Computer
sections.content:
The 4004 had one fundamental limitation: it processed only 4 bits per cycle. In a world where the standard for text processing was 8-bit ASCII codes, this was like walking on one leg. The industry needed a processor that could handle a full "byte" in a single pass.

Intel answered in April 1972 with the 8008: the world's first 8-bit microprocessor. The story of the 8008's birth held an important lesson. A company called CTC (later DataPoint) wanted to build a desktop computer for small businesses: the DataPoint 2200. They approached Intel to design the processor, and their requirements directly shaped the 8008's architecture. Intel built the 8008 to be the beating heart of that computer.

But fate, once again, charted a different course. The first 8008 samples arrived late, and their performance — due to the use of slow PMOS technology — was unsatisfactory. The engineers at CTC, tired of waiting, built their machine using around a hundred discrete TTL chips and set the 8008 aside. Thus, the first attempt to build a personal computer around a microprocessor ended in relative failure.

But the 8008 taught the industry an enormous lesson: an 8-bit microprocessor could, conceptually, serve as the core of a complete computer. The path was now open.

The lessons of the 4004 and the 8008 — one a triumph, the other a near-failure — led Intel to design a processor that would change everything. In April 1974, Intel brought the 8080 to market: faster NMOS technology, a clock speed of 2 megahertz, and a rich instruction set. But the true genius of the 8080 was not in its hardware; it was in Intel's open approach. They published complete documentation and explicitly invited other companies to build compatible peripheral chips. This move created a vast market of memory chips, controllers, and I/O ports — all revolving around the 8080.

The fruit of this open ecosystem ripened in January 1975. Popular Electronics magazine revealed a device on its cover called the Altair 8800: a computer based on the 8080, offered as a kit for $439. The reaction was beyond anything imagined. Tens of thousands of orders poured in from engineers, students, and hobbyists who had never before had access to a computer.

The Altair became the birthplace of a social movement. In garages and basements, users built hardware for it and shared their designs in magazines like BYTE. Two young students named Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote a BASIC interpreter for the Altair — and this became the foundation stone of a tiny company called Micro-Soft.

But the Altair's most important legacy was something Gary Kildall created. Kildall, a quiet university professor with a Ph.D. in computer science, wrote an operating system called CP/M. The genius of CP/M was this: a standard software layer that sat between application programs and different hardware. A programmer could write a word processor like WordStar once and be certain it would run on any machine with CP/M.

CP/M rapidly became the dominant standard for business computers. And this created an enormous strategic asset for the 8080 architecture: a vast library of business software that practically only ran on 8080-compatible processors. It was no longer hardware that sold the computer; it was software. Companies bought computers to run WordStar and VisiCalc. Any processor that wanted to be taken seriously in the market had to conquer this software territory.

sections.title: A Different Vision — and a Rebellion from Pennsylvania
sections.content:
Just as the 8080 was conquering the market, a completely different vision emerged from Motorola: the 6800 processor. If the 8080 was the symbol of an open and sometimes chaotic ecosystem, the 6800 was the embodiment of order, integration, and engineering elegance.

Motorola's team, led by Tom Bennett — who had glimpsed the original idea from Ted Hoff — insisted on different principles. The 6800 needed only a single +5V power supply, whereas the 8080 required three different voltages. This simplicity meant lower cost, higher reliability, and easier power supply design. The 6800's internal architecture was also symmetric and logical, making assembly-language programming intuitive and less error-prone. But most importantly, Motorola took a "system on a chip" approach: they introduced the 6800 not as a standalone chip, but as the central core of the "M6800 family" — a complete set of memory and interface chips that worked together naturally.

Federico Faggin, the architect of the 8080, admitted with respect: "The 6800 has a better architecture. It's a cleaner machine."

But the 6800 had two weak points: a higher price, and the absence of the enormous software ecosystem the 8080 had inherited through CP/M. Motorola never conquered the personal computer market, but it remained unrivaled elsewhere: industry. Point-of-sale terminals, early ATMs, and industrial controllers — places where durability and reliability mattered more than raw processing power — became the unchallenged domain of the 6800.

The market now had two powerful poles: Intel, with a vast software ecosystem but relatively complex hardware; and Motorola, with a beautiful, integrated design that was expensive and lacked business software. It was as if the industry was waiting for a synthesis of the two.

But before that could happen, an earthquake from Pennsylvania caught everyone off guard.

Chuck Peddle, a self-taught engineer and former soldier with a rebellious spirit, had been one of the 6800's designers at Motorola. When Motorola's management kept the 6800's price high, Peddle could not bear it. He told his colleague Bill Mensch: "These people think a processor is a luxury item. But I know it's the foundation stone of the future. It needs to be so cheap that any school student can buy one."

In the spring of 1974, Peddle and Mensch left Motorola and joined a small, obscure company called MOS Technology in Pennsylvania. There, in a windowless room, on a shoestring budget, they began to work. Peddle led brainstorming sessions with shouts: "Cut this section! What does the customer really want? Cheapness and efficiency!" Mensch, silent and focused, drew the new architecture on paper using the absolute minimum of transistors.

The result was unveiled in September 1975 at the Atlantic City exhibition: the MOS 6502. The price? Twenty-five dollars. While the 8080 cost about $175.

A wave of shock, and then excitement, swept through the hall. Young engineers surrounded the MOS booth. One of them was Steve Wozniak, who bought several samples and, in his father's garage, built a computer with one. His friend Steve Jobs insisted they sell it. They called it the Apple I — and this was the spark that built Apple. Later, Commodore placed the 6502 at the heart of the best-selling personal computer in history, the Commodore 64, and into the Atari 2600 game console.

Peddle had proven that a low price was itself a form of power. But the 6502 was not compatible with the 8080 — this processor belonged to a parallel world, the world of consumers and games, not the CP/M-dominated business market. Kildall's software empire remained untouched.

sections.title: Coup in the Shadows
sections.content:
In Federico Faggin's office at Intel, the atmosphere was heavy. He was the architect of the 4004 and the 8080, a man with silicon dust flowing through his veins. He had come from Italy to live the dream of building integrated circuits, and now his greatest achievement — the 8080 — had conquered the market.

But Intel's management, led by Gordon Moore and Andy Grove, saw the future differently. Their strategy was focused on semiconductor memories, and they regarded the microprocessor as a side activity. They refused to invest seriously in the next generation.

Faggin was furious at this shortsightedness. In the autumn of 1974, he made his decision. He went to Ralph Ungermann, a clever and ambitious executive, and in a simple restaurant in Palo Alto, he said: "Ralph, we are building the future, but they only see the past. I want to build a company focused on one thing and one thing only: building the best microprocessor in the world. Not good — the best."

Ungermann agreed. With investment from the oil company Exxon, Zilog was founded in November 1974. The name came from "Z-integrated logic," and Z — the last letter of the alphabet — seemed to signal a determination to build the last, the ultimate processor.

But Faggin was not alone. He went to Masatoshi Shima. Shima, the brilliant Japanese engineer who had worked alongside Faggin to build the 8080's architecture, was now back in Japan. Faggin sat across from him in a Japanese restaurant and, without preamble, said: "Shima-san, we want to finish what we started with the 8080. A processor that is not only better than the 8080 — but better than anything that exists. You must come with us." Shima, without a moment's hesitation, bowed his head in assent.

The golden circle was complete: Faggin, Shima, and Ungermann. Three men with three complementary forces: vision, precision, and management. They gathered in Zilog's small office in Cupertino and wrote down three principles that would alter the course of history:

1. Full compatibility: The new processor must be binary-compatible with the 8080. The entire CP/M software empire — WordStar, dBASE, and whatever came next — had to run on the new chip without the slightest change. This was an inheritance that could not be ignored.
2. Absolute superiority: They must not simply build a faster 8080. They had to improve on everything: more registers, more powerful instructions, higher speed, and — the great lesson of the 6800 — a single +5V supply. The new processor had to combine the best of both worlds: the ecosystem power of the 8080, and the engineering elegance of the 6800.
3. A price to shock the market: Not so low that they entered a futile war with the 6502 in the consumer market (the CP/M business market was the target, not game consoles), but competitive enough to tempt customers of Intel's 8080 and 8085 to migrate.

The year 1976 began. On the surface, everything in the industry appeared calm. Intel was working on the 8085 — an attempt to bring single-voltage supply to the 8080 architecture, designed precisely to counter the 6800's advantage. Motorola still relied on its elegant but expensive 6800. MOS was tearing through the consumer market with the 6502. And the CP/M empire, with unshakeable loyalty to the 8080 architecture, ruled the world of business software.

But in Zilog's office, the silence meant nothing but pure concentration. Faggin and Shima bent over silicon layouts day and night. They had only one chance, and they knew it.

On a spring evening in March 1976, Faggin finished his final review. He rose from his desk, walked to the window, and stared at the quiet street beyond the glass. Then, turning to Shima and his small team, he said with the calm that comes from certainty: "It's done. We have it."

He paused, and then, his voice slightly louder: "Now they must know that a new king has arrived."

The Z80 was now born. And nothing would ever be the same again.

sections.title: The Silicon Magic — Z80 Architecture Under the Microscope
sections.content:
Let us take a step back and think about what a processor truly was in 1976. A modern chip today holds billions of transistors. The Z80 had just eight thousand five hundred. For comparison, the 8080 had four thousand eight hundred, and the 6800 had four thousand one hundred. With this limited count, Shima and Faggin had to resort to a kind of engineering sorcery to fit everything they had in mind onto a rectangle of silicon roughly four by four millimeters.

Imagine you are cooking dinner in a busy kitchen. On the counter in front of you, your chopped ingredients are laid out: onions, garlic, herbs, meat. Suddenly, the phone rings. In an ordinary kitchen, you would have to gather up all your ingredients, set them aside, answer the phone, and then come back and arrange everything from scratch.

Registers in a processor are exactly that front counter. The data currently being processed is held right there. The 8080 had seven of these counters. The 6800 had just two. The 6502 had three.

When an interrupt occurred — say, a user pressed a key, or data arrived from a disk — the processor had to suspend its current work, send the contents of the registers one by one to memory (which was slow and costly), handle the interrupt, and then restore everything. This process could take dozens of clock cycles.

Shima offered a solution that was both brilliant and simple: two complete rows of counters. One for current work, the other for emergencies. They called them the shadow registers. The first set contained BC, DE, HL, AF. The second set held BC', DE', HL', AF'. The apostrophe marked the backup version.

Now, when an interrupt arrived, a single instruction was enough: EXX. Just four clock cycles. And the entire contents of the first row swapped with the second. It was as if you had swapped out your entire kitchen with a single click. No shuttling back and forth to memory, no wasted time. Engineers working on real-time systems — industrial controllers, medical equipment, telephone switches — saw this feature not as a luxury but as a vital necessity.

But Faggin went one step further. He designed a separate instruction for swapping only the AF register pair with AF': EX AF, AF'. Why? Because the Flags were held in the F register — bits that indicated whether the result of the last operation was zero, negative, or had overflowed. Sometimes you only needed to save the flag status, not everything. The Z80 let you do exactly what you needed — no more, no less.

Now imagine you are searching for a book in a large library. The shelf you want is Row 12, Tier 3, and the fourth book from the left. If the library had a system that said, start at shelf 12, then go to tier 3, then take the fourth book, your task would be simple. You would not need to calculate the exact shelf address from scratch every time.

Index Registers do exactly this. You place a base address in them — the start of a table or an array, say — and then, with a small number called an offset, you can access any point in that table.

Motorola's 6800 had one index register, and this single feature made programming data structures far simpler than on the 8080. The 8080 had no index register at all. To access the nth element of an array, you had to load the starting address into HL, load the value n separately, add them together, and then go to that address. A programming nightmare.

The Z80 brought two index registers: IX and IY. Two, not one. Why two? Because in real programs, you often work with two data structures at once: one array for input, one for output. Or a lookup table and a buffer for storing results. With IX and IY, both were available simultaneously.

Shima designed a complete set of instructions for these registers. You could work with 8-bit offsets (from -128 to +127). You could load any 8-bit register into the location pointed to by IX, or do the reverse. You could perform arithmetic directly on data sitting at the address IX+offset. This level of flexibility existed in no other 8-bit processor.

Now think about one of the most tedious programming tasks on the 8080: copying a block of a hundred bytes from one place in memory to another. On the 8080, you had to write something like this: load a byte from the HL address, store it at the DE address, increment HL, increment DE, decrement the counter, and if not finished, jump back. Five instructions forming a loop. A hundred bytes meant those five instructions had to execute a hundred times.

The Z80 needed just one instruction: LDIR. LoaD, Increment, Repeat. One instruction. One line of code. The processor knew on its own how many times to do this (the count was stored in BC), incremented the addresses itself, and knew when to stop.

CPIR was similar, but for searching: ComPare, Increment, Repeat. Searching for a specific byte among thousands? One instruction sufficed. It was as though the Z80 had a built-in search engine.

These block instructions did not just save the programmer's time. They also dramatically increased speed. Because the loop ran inside the processor itself, there was none of the repeated back-and-forth to memory for fetching instructions. Zilog's engineers calculated that LDIR ran up to four times faster than its 8080 equivalent for large blocks.

sections.title: Bit Surgery, Relative Jumps, and the Invisible Soldier
sections.content:
On the 8080, if you wanted to set the third bit of a register to one, what did you have to do? You created a mask (for example, 00001000), ORed it with the register, and stored the result back. Multiple instructions, and along the way, you had to save the previous contents of the register somewhere.

The Z80 had a complete set of bit-oriented instructions: BIT (test a bit), SET (set a bit to one), RES (reset a bit to zero). Each could operate on any bit of any 8-bit register. You could even execute them directly on data sitting at the address pointed to by IX or IY, without first moving that data into a register.

For programmers writing industrial control systems, this was as essential as daily bread. Imagine a sensor connected to an input port, reporting the status of eight different devices in a single byte. Bit 3 corresponds to the furnace temperature. With the Z80, you could directly say: BIT 3, A. If bit 3 was on, the furnace was hot. No mask, no intermediate operations.

On the 8080, all jumps were absolute. You had to write the exact destination address into the code. If you wanted to say, if the result was zero, go forward ten bytes, you had to calculate exactly where in memory ten bytes forward would land. This meant your code was dependent on its location in memory. Programs were hard — you could not easily relocate them.

The Z80 brought the JR instruction: Jump Relative. Instead of an absolute address, you gave a small signed number (from -128 to +127). If zero, go forward ten. If not, go back five. Now a program could be loaded anywhere in memory and still work correctly. This feature was vital for an operating system like CP/M, which needed to load programs at different memory addresses.

And now we come to perhaps the most clever trick of the Z80: the R register, or Refresh Register.

DRAM memories, which were rapidly gaining popularity in the 1970s, worked on the basis of tiny capacitors that held an electrical charge — charged meant 1, empty meant 0. But these capacitors lost their charge within a few milliseconds. Like a bucket with a leak. To prevent data from vanishing, every memory cell had to be periodically read and rewritten. This was called Refresh.

In 8080-based systems, a separate circuit on the board had to perform this task. That circuit added extra cost, took up space, and was itself a potential source of failure. The situation was the same with the 6800 and 6502.

Faggin thought: the processor itself is constantly accessing memory. Why not use those very accesses for Refresh? The R register was a 7-bit counter that incremented with every instruction fetch from memory. Its upper seven bits — which were constantly changing — were connected to the upper address lines of the bus, and in this way, all rows of DRAM memory were automatically and continuously refreshed.

The beauty of this solution was that it was completely free. The processor was accessing memory anyway. Refresh was merely a byproduct of those accesses. It required no extra hardware, no extra software, not even a single extra clock cycle.

For system builders, this meant eliminating an entire chip from the board. Lower cost, less complexity, higher reliability. The Z80, all by itself, did what had previously required two chips. This silent integration was perhaps more important than all its new instructions combined, because it directly affected the final price of the product.

sections.title: When Numbers Speak — The Comparison Table
sections.content:
Let us lay the Z80 against its rivals on paper, once and for all. Not for argument, but to understand why this chip was different.

Intel 8080 (1974): 4,800 transistors. Required three voltages: +5V, +12V, and -5V. No built-in clock oscillator. Seven general-purpose registers. Zero index registers. Seventy-eight instructions. No DRAM refresh. Initial price around $149, dropping to about $60 in volume by 1977.

Intel 8085 (1976): 6,500 transistors. Single +5V supply. Built-in clock oscillator. Still seven registers, still seventy-eight instructions, still no index registers, still no DRAM refresh. Intel had tried to build a modernized 8080, while the Z80 was a complete rethinking.

Motorola 6800 (1974): 4,100 transistors. Single +5V supply. No built-in clock. Two general-purpose registers. One index register. Seventy-two instructions. No DRAM refresh. Beautiful, clean architecture — but expensive at $175 initial, around $60 in volume.

MOS 6502 (1975): 3,510 transistors. Single +5V supply. No built-in clock. Three general-purpose registers. Zero index registers. Fifty-six instructions. No DRAM refresh. The cheapest of all at $25 initial, dropping to an astonishing $15 in volume.

Zilog Z80 (1976): 8,500 transistors. Single +5V supply. Built-in clock oscillator. Fourteen general-purpose registers across two banks. Two index registers (IX and IY). One hundred fifty-eight instructions. Built-in DRAM refresh. Full 8080 binary compatibility. Initial price $200, dropping to about $50 in volume.

Look at the last row. The 6502 at fifteen dollars was the cheapest. But look at the rows above: zero index registers, no built-in refresh, no clock oscillator, only fifty-six instructions. This processor was perfect for a $300 home computer — and that is exactly why the Apple II and Commodore 64 used it. But for a business system that needed to run a database, handle a heavy word processor, and serve multiple users simultaneously? No.

Now let us calculate the real cost of a complete system. This was the calculation engineers at computer manufacturers performed.

A 6502-based system: processor $15, external clock oscillator $8, DRAM refresh circuit $12, power supply and miscellaneous support components $20. Total: $55.

A Z80-based system: processor $50, clock oscillator $0 (built-in), DRAM refresh $0 (built-in), power supply and miscellaneous support components $15 (because it was single-voltage and simpler design). Total: $65.

The real difference was only ten dollars. Ten dollars for a processor with twice the registers, three times the instructions, and the ability to run the entire CP/M software library. From the perspective of a business system manufacturer, that ten dollars was the best investment of a lifetime.

The Z80 had another hidden layer that no table could capture: interrupts. The 8080 had a simple interrupt system. When an external device wanted the processor's attention, it sent a signal. The processor stopped its current work and jumped to a fixed address. Only one type of interrupt, only one address.

The Z80 had three interrupt modes. Mode 0: exactly like the 8080, for full compatibility. Mode 1: the simplest mode. An interrupt occurred and the processor jumped to address 0038h. For very simple systems with only one interrupting device. And Mode 2: this was the real magic. In this mode, the external device placed an 8-bit vector onto the data bus. The Z80 combined this vector with the contents of the I register (another 8-bit register that you had set beforehand) to form a 16-bit address. It then went to that address, read a 16-bit word, and jumped to the address contained in that word.

The result: you could have 128 different devices, each with its own interrupt, and each with its own separate service routine. The Z80 had a fully vectored interrupt system, without needing any external interrupt controller. For computers dealing with disk drives, printers, keyboards, and serial ports, this was a blessing.

sections.title: The Battle in the Market — and Beyond the Iron Curtain
sections.content:
By the end of 1976, the Z80 had transformed from an engineering project into a real product. But selling a processor is different from selling an ordinary commodity. You have to bring an entire ecosystem along with you: hardware manufacturers to design their boards around your processor, programmers to write code for it, and customers willing to risk migrating from an established platform.

The Z80 had one enormous trump card: CP/M. Gary Kildall, the creator of this operating system, quickly recognized the Z80's potential. CP/M not only ran on the Z80 — it ran faster, thanks to the new instructions. Kildall optimized a version of CP/M for the Z80, and that meant the entire vast library of business software — WordStar, dBASE II, SuperCalc, and dozens of other programs — was available for the Z80 overnight.

The first commercial computer with a Z80 was built by Cromemco. Roger Melen, Cromemco's founder, was one of those early customers who walked into Zilog's office and bought two chips. The Cromemco Z-1 shipped in late 1976, and although its price was high at $2,495, it proved that the Z80 worked in a real product.

But the main wave was launched by another company: Radio Shack. The TRS-80, introduced in August 1977 at $599, placed the Z80 at its heart. Radio Shack had five thousand stores across America, and the TRS-80 quickly became the best-selling personal computer of 1977 through 1979. The Z80 was no longer just an interesting chip for engineers; it was becoming a household name.

That same year, Japanese companies that had previously only watched now joined the line. NEC obtained an official license for the Z80 and began building its own version: the μPD780. Toshiba, Sharp, and Hitachi followed. The Z80 was becoming a global standard.

Meanwhile, Intel had released the 8085 and was trying to reclaim the market. The 8085 had dropped its price to $30 in volume, and on pure chip cost, it was cheaper than the Z80. But it was already too late. The CP/M ecosystem was now practically optimized for the Z80. Computer manufacturers preferred to pay ten dollars more for the processor and gain access to all that software, rather than buy cheaper and be shut out of the software world.

By 1978, industry analysts wrote that the Z80 had captured over sixty percent of the desktop 8-bit processor market. This number, for an eleven-person company just two years old, was staggering.

And then something strange happened. The Z80 crossed beyond the borders of the Western world.

In the Soviet Union, processors were not merely electronic components. They were strategic goods whose export to the Eastern Bloc was under strict control. But the Soviets wanted the Z80 — and they found their own way to get it. They obtained samples of the Z80 from the open market, chemically stripped away the layers, extracted the design, and built their own version. The result was a processor coded KP580IK80. This Soviet version had minor changes: maximum frequency was limited to 2.5 megahertz instead of the original Z80's 4 megahertz, and some peripheral features were removed. But at its core, it was the same Z80.

The Eastern Bloc countries — East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Romania — all built their own versions of the Z80. In East Germany, the Microelectronics Combine Erfurt produced the U880 processor, which remained in production until the fall of the Berlin Wall. Interestingly, the U880 was in some respects better than the early Z80 samples — it tolerated higher frequencies and consumed less power.

The Z80 had become a processor that knew no walls. Not the walls of commercial competition, not the walls of engineering, and not even the Berlin Wall.

By late 1978, less than three years after Zilog's founding, the Z80 had become an empire. From business computers in New York offices to industrial controllers in Stuttgart factories, from arcade cabinets in Tokyo to military equipment on both sides of the Iron Curtain — the Z80 was everywhere.

Faggin had achieved what he set out to do: the Z80 was the undisputed king of the 8-bit world. But he was clever enough to know that this reign would not last forever. On the horizon, a storm was gathering: the 16-bit world. Intel introduced the 8086 in June 1978. Motorola's 68000 arrived in 1979. Zilog itself designed the Z8000 — a 16-bit processor that, although it never matched the Z80's success, showed that Faggin and his team had their eyes on the future.

But that is a story for Chapter Three. For now, in this moment in history, in late 1978, the Z80 sat on the throne. A processor built by three rebels on a shoestring budget with a team of eleven now pulsed at the heart of millions of devices across the world. And it would continue to beat for another fifty years.
